subject: Computer Networking
title: Hashing: Digital Fingerprints
description: Learn Hashing: Digital Fingerprints in one minute.

hook.text: Change one letter in a document and the hash changes completely. That's how you know data hasn't been tampered with.

buildup.text: A hash function takes any input and produces a fixed-size output. SHA-256 always gives a 256-bit fingerprint.

discovery.text: Hashing is one-way. You can't reverse the hash to get the original data. That makes it perfect for passwords.

twist.text: Two inputs producing the same hash is a collision. Good hash functions make collisions astronomically unlikely.

climax.text: Blockchains, password storage, file integrity checks, and digital signatures all depend on reliable hashing.

punchline.text: A hash proves data is unchanged. One bit different, totally different hash.

quiz.question: What property makes hash functions useful for password storage?
options: They are one-way — you can't reverse them to get the original input
They compress passwords to save storage space
They encrypt passwords with a secret key

details.summary: Hashing transforms any input into a fixed-length output called a digest or hash that uniquely identifies the original data. Even a single-bit change produces a completely different hash. Hashes verify data integrity, store passwords safely, and underpin digital signatures and blockchain.
details.whyItMatters: Hashing is the foundation of data integrity verification across all of computing. Password storage, file verification, digital signatures, and blockchain all depend on the properties of hash functions.
takeaways: Hash functions produce fixed-length outputs from any size input
Even tiny input changes produce completely different hash values
SHA-256 is the current standard for cryptographic hashing

faq.question: How are passwords stored using hashes?
faq.answer: Systems store the hash of your password, not the password itself. When you log in, the system hashes your input and compares it to the stored hash. Even if the database is stolen, attackers get hashes, not passwords. Salting adds random data before hashing to prevent precomputed attacks.

faq.question: Can two different inputs produce the same hash?
faq.answer: Theoretically yes — this is called a collision. Secure hash functions like SHA-256 make collisions so astronomically unlikely that finding one intentionally would take more energy than the sun produces. Older algorithms like MD5 and SHA-1 have known collision vulnerabilities and should not be used.
